prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that many atoms can be interrogated without perturbation, reaching fractional uncertainties of the order of 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The exchange has made me more confident, not less, because every member who objected to B007 objected on novelty or timing, and none disputed the experimental record. What I look for is the original experiment and the people who did it. The original idea is the magic-wavelength lattice, in which the trap wavelength is chosen so that the light shift is the same for both clock states. Katori's group put forward and developed it in 2001-2003 and went on to the first strontium lattice-clock demonstrations. Ye's group then used the many-atom lattice to reach the 10^-18 regime and showed the many-body systematics. The result is verified in the strongest sense, since JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and NPL build such clocks and their comparisons, including over fibre links, agree. It also opens a door: millimetre-scale redshift measurements, constraints on drifting constants and dark matter, and a route to a new definition of the second. In answer to the chair, my proposed wording separates the achievement from earlier prizes by naming the principle (magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms in an optical lattice) and not 'optical clocks' in general, so it does not overlap the 2005 comb or 2012 ion-control citations and does not claim the ion clocks. On waiting for the redefinition of the second, my position is that we should not wait. The prize is for a discovery or invention, and its verification is independent clock comparison, not a decision by a metrology body.
statement.case_against: The reservations are real and I do not want to understate them. First, a reader can say that the comb (2005) and ion control (2012) already covered precision frequency metrology and that this is an evolutionary gain of several orders of magnitude. I think the answer lies in the citation, but I accept that a member who reads the prize criteria more strictly, as a new phenomenon and not a better measurement, can reasonably vote differently, and I record that Danielsson and Mehlig hold something close to that view. Second, priority has not been checked against primary records inside this process. Lemonde, Derevianko and Pal'chikov contributed to magic-wavelength and light-shift ideas, and the Sr, Yb and Al+ groups at NIST, PTB and SYRTE were part of the field, so some outside check of the 2001-2003 proposal and the first lattice-clock papers should be requested before the citation is fixed. Third, a prize to two names for a technique implemented in many laboratories will leave some people feeling excluded, which I regard as a cost, not a defect in the physics. Fourth, I have been asked as an atomic-adjacent member to check the record, but I am an electron microscopist and must be candid that my check is of the published chronology as I know it, not an expert review.

responses.point: Stefan restates that B007 is the cleanest measurement case, that the citation should say 'at the 10^-18 level' without naming a single record, and that some members may prefer to wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree on both wording points: the citation should say 'of the order of 10^-18' and not name a record, since the best values change every year, and it should name the lattice principle. I also hold my round-1 position against waiting. If we made the prize depend on the CGPM timetable we would be rewarding an administrative step and not the original work. Where I still disagree with Stefan's earlier suggestion of pairing B007 with a second part such as B043 or B012 is on room: with Katori and Ye taking two of the three seats, a second part can have only one name, and none of the candidates offered has a defensible single-person credit. I would therefore keep the prize to one part.

responses.point: Mark, our chair, moved from B012 to B007, keeps B012 as his first alternative, and says that if the committee wants a discovery about nature and not an instrument, B012 is the stronger candidate and should not be lost. He also asked that the citation name the lattice technique and not optical clocks generally.
responses.response: I take his wording request as adopted: my citation names magic-wavelength trapping in an optical lattice. On whether B007 is an instrument and not a discovery, I think the distinction is less sharp than it looks. A tool that lets us see something previously invisible is what I mean by opening a door, and the lattice clock has already measured the gravitational redshift over millimetres in the laboratory. I agree that B012 should not be lost, and I keep it as an alternative. But I share his own difficulty with it: a collaboration result with AMANDA and DUMAND precursors and source evidence at about four sigma, with no agreed two-name credit. Until the original work in the diffuse-flux analysis is attributed to named people, I cannot put it in a configuration.

responses.point: Ulf holds B012 first but says its support is thin, that attribution is its main weakness, that he leans against Yoshida, and that B007 is the candidate that can actually get a broad majority. He asks whether the committee should accept the clearest-attribution, broadest-support option over a stronger discovery case.
responses.response: I respect that he states the weakness of his own case before anyone else does. I do not select B007 because it has support. I select it because the discovery, the verification and the names are each defensible, and the support count is a consequence. His point that a new window on the universe is the stronger kind of discovery is fair, and if the IceCube credit were resolved I would reconsider. Two names, Halzen and Karle, is a smaller and more defensible set than the shortlisted three, and I agree with his lean on Yoshida. But the question I would put to him is which of the two conceived the ice-based detector and which made it work, and whether the 2013 discovery analysis can be attributed to either. Without that answer, I keep B012 second among my alternatives, not in the configuration.

responses.point: Olle left his opening choice B018 for B007, but notes that he still feels the pull of condensed-matter candidates (B018 DMFT, B005 twisted bilayer graphene) and does not want a strong metrology case to crowd them out. He raises the open pairing mechanism and sample dependence of B005.
responses.response: I share his concern about not letting breadth of support crowd out condensed matter, which is why B005 is my first alternative. I ranked it third in my opening. My difficulty in a one-part prize is the credit: Yuan Cao carried out the 2018 experiments and is not among the credited names, and with three seats already shared Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero leave no room. I also agree with his own assessment of the pairing mechanism and the device dependence, which is a maturity question separate from priority. I would not add B005 as a second part now, but I would welcome it in a later year if the experimental credit can be settled. As for B018, the Metzner omission seems to me a fairness problem that cannot be fixed within the credited-name limit.

uncertainties: Exact priority between Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice demonstrations and the contemporaneous work of Ye's group and others has not been verified from primary sources in this process, and I request that an outside expert check it before the citation is fixed.

Whether the committee as a whole regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I judge that they are, but I recognise the opposite reading as legitimate.

Whether Lemonde, Derevianko, Pal'chikov or the ion-clock groups have a claim so strong that the two-name credit would be unfair; the three-person cap leaves one seat open but I know of no third name I can defend as decisive.
Whether the IceCube credit (B012) and the twisted bilayer graphene credit (B005) could be resolved by expert reports well enough for either to become a second part in future years.
statement.conflict_note: No personal conflict. I disclose, as in round 1, that I hold a Fellowship at the University of Tokyo and have long-running exchanges with the Tokyo, Kyushu and Tohoku microscopy communities, and that Katori is associated with the University of Tokyo and RIKEN. I have no collaboration or co-authorship with Katori, Ye or any other shortlisted candidate, and I regard this as an institutional acquaintance that does not require recusal. My Chalmers colleague Johansson has disclosed his closeness to B044, which is not part of my configuration.
